strategy_title: Autotune Larger Block Size to Eliminate Partial Wave
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512, 1024, 2048) to eliminate a partial-wave tail caused a 3.1x regression despite improving compute throughput (33% → 76%) and occupancy (62% → 85%). The critical failure was that the grid size remained fixed at 3920 (the original cdiv(xnumel, 128) value) instead of being updated to a lambda that adapts to the autotuned XBLOCK, causing 7.42 waves per SM instead of the intended ~3.7 waves and inflating executed instructions from 1.35M to 9.33M (7x more work). When adding autotune, the launch grid must also be updated to a meta-lambda; a static grid computed from the old block size will over-launch blocks and repeat work.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: static grid, fixed XBLOCK
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # = 3920 blocks
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)

# AFTER (broken): autotune added but grid not updated
@triton.autotune(configs=[Config({'XBLOCK': 512}), Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}), ...])
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr): ...

grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # BUG: still 3920, not adapted to XBLOCK
kernel[grid](...)  # launches 3920 blocks even when XBLOCK=512 → 7x over-launch
applicable_when: Never apply this specific pattern (static grid + autotune XBLOCK) — it is always wrong. The corrected version (meta-lambda grid) is applicable when: LaunchConfiguration rule fires with >20% speedup_pct, waves_per_sm < 4, and the kernel has low register pressure (< 32 registers/thread) leaving headroom for larger blocks.
do_not_apply_when: Do not use a static grid expression computed from a fixed block size when adding @triton.autotune that varies XBLOCK. The grid must always be a meta-lambda. Also avoid increasing block size when registers_per_thread would exceed ~32 at the larger block size, as this reduces Block Limit Registers and caps occupancy.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: @triton.autotune requires the launch grid to be a callable (lambda meta: ...) that reads meta['XBLOCK'] to compute the correct grid dimension. A static grid tuple computed before the kernel call will not adapt to the autotuned config and will over-launch blocks, causing each element to be processed multiple times.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK to Eliminate Partial Wave Tail
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512, 1024, 2048) to a pointwise kernel caused a regression (0.85x) despite improving scheduler eligibility (No Eligible: 41% → 18%) and occupancy (62% → 74%). The autotuner selected a config that nearly doubled register usage per thread (18 → 32), which increased total executed instructions by ~86% (1.35M → 2.51M) and extended kernel duration from 5.06 µs to 5.98 µs. The grid was not updated to use a lambda (META['XBLOCK']) — it remained hardcoded at cdiv(xnumel, 128) = 3920 blocks — so the larger XBLOCK configs ran with the same grid size, causing each thread block to process more elements than intended and inflating instruction count without reducing block count. The structural anti-pattern is adding @triton.autotune without also changing the grid launch to use `lambda META: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, META['XBLOCK']),)`, which means the grid size does not shrink when XBLOCK grows.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: hardcoded XBLOCK=128, grid fixed
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # 3920 blocks
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Pointwise kernels with a partial-wave tail (LaunchConfiguration NCU rule), low register usage (<24 registers/thread), no shared memory, and a fixed small XBLOCK (e.g. 128) that produces many small blocks.
do_not_apply_when: The grid launch is not updated to use a META lambda alongside the autotune decorator — this causes the grid to remain at the original small-XBLOCK size while the kernel body processes more elements, inflating instruction count and causing regression. Also avoid when register count is already near the per-SM limit, as larger XBLOCK configs may push register usage up and reduce occupancy.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune MUST be paired with a lambda grid `lambda META: (triton.cdiv(N, META['XBLOCK']),)` so the grid shrinks as XBLOCK grows. Passing a static grid tuple with a hardcoded cdiv(N, 128) while autotuning XBLOCK is an implementation flaw that causes the kernel to over-process elements.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK to eliminate partial wave tail
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune to explore larger XBLOCK values (512, 1024, 2048) to reduce grid size and eliminate partial-wave tail caused a regression. Although occupancy improved (62% → 74%) and scheduler idle slots dropped (41% → 18%), registers per thread jumped from 18 to 32, nearly doubling total executed instructions (1.35M → 2.51M) and increasing elapsed cycles by 15%. The autotuner selected a config that increased register pressure and instruction count enough to outweigh the partial-wave elimination benefit, resulting in a net 13.6% slowdown. When the kernel has very low register usage (≤18/thread) and the partial-wave tail is the flagged bottleneck, simply adding autotune without controlling register pressure can cause the compiler to spill or expand register file usage at larger tile sizes, negating the wave-elimination gain.
applicable_when: Kernel has LaunchConfiguration rule triggered with large partial-wave tail AND registers per thread remain stable (do not increase) at larger XBLOCK values
do_not_apply_when: Autotune causes registers per thread to increase significantly (e.g., 18 → 32); when the grid lambda is not updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] so the grid size does not actually shrink; when instruction count more than doubles at larger tile sizes
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune must be paired with a lambda grid (e.g., lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)) to actually reduce grid size. In this case the grid was NOT updated to use meta['XBLOCK'], so the grid remained 3920 blocks regardless of the autotuned XBLOCK — the partial wave was never eliminated. The register increase from 18 to 32 suggests the larger XBLOCK caused the compiler to use more registers, reducing the occupancy benefit and increasing instruction count.

strategy_title: Increasing Block Size With Fixed Grid Inflates Instruction Count
strategy_description: Increasing block size from 128 to 512 (via autotune) while keeping the grid fixed at 3920 blocks caused a 1.85x regression: executed instructions ballooned from 1.18M to 4.71M (4x), and kernel duration grew from 5.09 µs to 9.34 µs. The grid was not updated to a meta-lambda, so the same 3920 blocks each processed 4x more elements than needed, repeating work. Although occupancy improved (56% → 76%) and compute throughput rose (29% → 64%), the 4x instruction inflation completely dominated, and a new CPIStall bottleneck appeared (46% of cycles stalled on warp not-selected). When the grid is not adapted to the new block size, larger blocks cause each SM to do proportionally more redundant work rather than fewer total blocks.
applicable_when: Never apply the broken pattern (static grid + autotune XBLOCK). The corrected meta-lambda pattern is applicable when LaunchConfiguration rule fires, waves_per_sm < 4, and registers_per_thread are stable across block sizes.
do_not_apply_when: Do not increase block size via autotune when the grid is not simultaneously updated to a meta-lambda. Also avoid when registers_per_thread are already at 32 and the kernel is not memory-bound, as the larger block size will create a CPIStall bottleneck from warp over-subscription without reducing total work.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: @triton.autotune that varies XBLOCK MUST be paired with a lambda grid `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(N, meta['XBLOCK']),)`. A static grid tuple computed from the original small XBLOCK will over-launch blocks proportionally to the XBLOCK increase ratio, multiplying executed instructions by the same factor. This is the same root cause as exp_001 items but confirmed again at iteration 5 with a different arithmetic optimization layered on top.
